Statement 
National Agricultural Research System 
The assessment of Research & Extension System is an on-going process 
and in-built mechanism in the system, both at Micro and Macro level. 
The agricultural research being done by the Institutes, National Bureaux, 
National Research Centres, Project Di rectorates and All India Coordinated 
Research Projects is periodically assessed at micro level by Quinquennial Review 
Team, Research Advisory Committee, St aff Research Council and Scientific 
Panels. On these Committees/Teams the eminent external subject- matter experts 
are nominated. 
The Macro level assessment is made periodically by eight Subject Matter 
Divisions functioning at Indian Council of Agricultural Research Headquarter, 
New Delhi; Director's Conference involving all the Directors of National 
Agriculture Research System; Vice-Ch ancellor's conference of all State 
Agricultural Universities; Project Co ordinators' Meeting and Steering Group 
& Working Group constitued by Planning Commission. 
As per the findings of these review mechanisms and the Steering/Working 
Group constituted by Planning Commission, the system has the capability 
enough to cope with the challenges faced by Indian Agriculture. As 
demonstrated in the past, the National Agricultural Research System has the 
potential, the ability and the will to make Indian agriculture most resilient and 
dynamic. 
1. In the post-independence period, the technolgoy back-up by the 
agricultural scientists coupled with positive policy support, and dedicated 
work of farmer have contributed  to the phenomenal increase in 
agricultural, animal and fish production in India. The Green, Blue, White 
and Yellow Revolutions bear testimony to the success of this strategy. 
We have been able to produce a record harvest of 209 million tonnes of 
food grains during 1999-2000. There has been a four-fold increase in the 
production of wheat, three-fold in rice, maize and cotton and two -fold in 
sugarcane, sorghum and oilseeds. The production of fruits and vegetables 
tripled during last fifty years. Meat production enhanced by six-fold and 
fish by seven-fold. The country became one of the largest milk producer 
and second in production of wheat, rice, onion, fruits & vegetables and 
sugarcane.

1% per annum over the last 25 years. 
3. The total agricultural exports, which were to the tune of Rs. 17496 crore

4. Another important indicator of the health and viability is its willingness to 
evaluate its weaknesses and equip itself. 
In the past, the Indian Agriculture has faced many challenges. From a 
food deficit State, the country became self-sufficient in food grain production. 
Now, the challenges before the Indian agriculture are: Doubling food production 
in current decade; increasing cropping intensity and productivity; Developing 
technology for arid agriculture and horticulture; Addressing second generation 
problem in Green Revolution areas; Sustaining the health of soil and other 
natural resources; Addressing the cost and quality issues; Development of 
farming modules suitable for small and marginal farmers; Gearing up the system 
to face WTO Regime and Globalisati on; and Maintaining standards of 
excellence and ethics in the performan ce of personnel to provide space for 
creativity and research.

been changing. So as to address these issues, the ICAR is providing due thrust 
to the following areas:

• Organic farming

• Post-production technologies and surplus management, particularly in 
milk, fruits and flowers

• Training of Scientists in sun-rise sectors 
• Continuous efforts to develop human resource to enhance its quality in 
general and in terms of values and ethics in particular 
• Focussed attention and specific efforts in far flung areas like NE Region, 
Andman & Nicobar for givng support to those dimensions of agriculture

Extension System   - 
Though the Agriculture being a State subject, the extension programmes 
are being implemented by respective St ates as well as Indian Council of 
Agricultural Research (ICAR) throgh its network of Krishi Vigyan Kendras 
(KVKs). The Division of Agricultural Extension of the ICAR and Department

of Agriculture and Cooperation periodically assess the refinement and 
dissemination of technology projects. 
An Assessment of Extension System was made at the time of formulation 
of National Agricultural Technology Project (N ATP-1995-96) funded by World 
Bank. The findings indicated that the Training & Visit (T&V) System of 
Extension operated in major States over two decades was found to be suited for 
dissemination of crop production practices, however lacked Farming System 
Approach and participatory methods and did not address to the diversification 
needs of the farmers, Research - Exte nsion-Farmer linkage remained weak. T 
& V System did not influence the technology dissemination in rainfed areas. 
To  address these issues and to bridge these gaps the Department of 
Agricultural Research and Education (DARE) launched a project on pilot basis 
at 70 centres viz. Technology Assessment and Refinement through Institution 
Village Linkage Programme (I VLP) and 40 Agricultural Technology Information 
Centres (ATIC). 
The Department of Agriculture and Cooperation has also taken up 
"Innovations in Technology Dissemination Component", under World Bank 
funded National Agricultural Techno logy Project. The project is being 
implemented in 7 States viz. Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, 
Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Orissa and Pu njab by establishing an Agricultural 
Technology Management Agency (ATMA). The ATMA has built in mechanisrh 
for assessment of gaps in the existing extension system through Farmers' 
Participatory Methodology and Development of Strategy to fill in these gaps 
by creation of a district level "Strateg ic Research and Extension Plan". The 
initial results obtained through various modes show that it has been showing 
encouraging results in terms of following milestones: 
• Adopting group approach to extension 
• Adopting bottom up planning procedures for setting location specific 
research and extension agenda. 
• Making the technology dissemination farmer driven and farmer 
accountable 
• Enabling public private partnership in technology dissemination 
• Moving towards integrated broad based extension delivery 
• Improving research-extension-farmer linkages

*22. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA': Will the Minister of YOUTH, 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a committee has been set up on Government - Industry co-
operation for promotion of sports: 
(b) if so, whether various sports federations are also associated with this 
committee; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SUSHREE 
UMA BHARTI): (a) to (c) A meeting was held on 7.12.2001 under the 
Chairmanship of the Union Finance Mi nister with the representatives of 
leading Chambers of Commerce and Industry to discuss the areas of cooperation

Growth target of agricultural sector 
*23. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state:— 
(a) the rate of growth targeted and achieved in agricultural sector during 
the last three years, year-wise; 
(b) whether it is a fact that this sector performed below the target during 
the same period; 
8 

[1 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) If so, the details thereof, togetherwith the reasons therefor; 
(d) The details of target set for the year 2001-02 and likely achievements 
thereof; and 
(d) The steps taken to improve the performance of this sector? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (d) A 
statement giving the targets and achievements of production of major crops in 
1998-99, 1999-2000, 2000-01 and 2001-02 is enclosed. It may be seen from 
the annexure that in most of the cases, the production has been lower than the 
targets. Achievement of targets in agriculture sector depends on various factors 
such as investment in agriculture, performance of monsoon, technological 
developments, timely application of quality inputs, dema nd for agricultural 
products etc. In particular, the agricultural production in the country is greatly 
influenced by the extent and spread of rainfall as about 62% of net area sown is 
dependent on rains for water. Deficient rainfall also adversely affects the irrigation 
potential. 
(e) In order to improve the performa nce of the agriculture sector, the 
Government have launched various new initiatives such as promotion of 
watershed development programmes, emphasis on developing and promoting 
new technologies, measures for increasin g availability of agricultural credit, 
credit linked subsidy scheme for augmenting storage/cold storage capacity. 
Technology Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture in North- 
Eastem States, Market Information Network and National Agriculture Insurance 
Scheme etc. Besides, the Government also encourages farmers to increase 
production through price policy which include implementation of Minimum 
Support Price and Market Intervention Schemes, procurement by public agencies 
and by using instruments of trade. Apart from these, the Government have also 
switched over from the conventional schematic approach to macro-management 
mode from November, 2000 for providing assistance to the States. The Macro- 
Management Scheme integrates 27 schemes into one for supplementing and 
complimenting the efforts of State Governments through work plans. This gives 
flexibility to States to address specific problem s faced by them depending on 
local requirements, avoid overlapping in the contents of different schemes and 
aim at all-round development of agriculture.

Purchase norms in Jaipur region of KVS 
†*24. SHRI D.P. YADAV: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is a definite procedural norm for purchases in Kendriya 
Vidyalaya Sangathan; if so, the details thereof and the amount above which 
tender is issued; 
(b) whether some group 'A 1 principals in Jaipur division have been 
accused of violation of procedure in purchase of computers and no action has 
been taken against them by the Sangathan, while some other principals have 
been punished for such violation; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) the justification for this discrimination; and 
(e) whether action is being taken against officials in Jaipur division 
accused of violation of procedure; if so, by when and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLIMANOHAR JOSH I): (a) to (e) Yes, Sir. Accounts Code for Kendriya 
Vidyalayas contains details of procedural norms for purchases. Normally for 
purchases exceeding Rs. 1000/-, tenders/quotations are necessary. However, in 
certain circumstances tenders/quotations need not be invited for purchases 
upto 5000/- on each occasion if it is not considered fe asible in the opinion of 
the competent authority. Some complaints were received regarding purchase of 
computers against Principal of KV, Naseerabad under Jaipur Region. On inquiry 
it was found that Principal had not obtained signatures of all purchase committee 
members on each paper of quotation letters and had not deducted 2% tax at 
source from the suppliers. These violations were not considered grave enough 
to take any punitive action against the Principal. According to KVS no complaint 
has been received against any one else regarding purchase of computers.

Women specific Schemes of Department of Women and Children 
1. Support to Training and Employment Programme for Women (STEP) 
This Programme launched in 1987, seeks to provide updated skills and new 
knowledge to poor and assetless women in the traditional sectors, such as, agriculture, 
animal husbandry, dairying, fisheries, handlooms, handicrafts, khadi

and village industries, sericulture, soci al forestry and wasteland development 
for enhancing their productivity and income generation. This would enhance 
and broaden their employm ent opportunities, including self-employment and 
development of entrepreneurial skills. Women beneficiaries are organised into 
viable and cohesive groups or co-operatives. A comprehensive package of 
services, such as, extension, inputs, ma rket linkages etc. are provided besides 
linkage with credit for transfer of assets. 
2. Women's Economic Programme (NORAD) 
This programme was launched in 1982-83 with assistance from Norwegian 
Agency for Development Cooperation (NORAD). Under this programme, 
financial assistance is given to Women's Development Corporations, Public 
Sector Corporations, autonomous bodies, and voluntary organisations, to train 
poor women, mostly in non-traditional trades and to ensure their employment in 
these areas. Some of the trades are computer programming, electronics, watch 
assembling, radio and television repairs, garment making, secretarial practices, 
community health work, embroidery, weaving, etc. Financial assistance is given 
to the grantee organisation for hiring of training-cum -production sheds, training 
costs, machinery and equipment, stipend to the trainees and remuneration for 
the trainers. 
3. Condensed Course of Education for Adult Women 
The Scheme of Condensed Course of Education for Women was started 
by the Central Social Welfare Board during the year 1958 with the objective of 
providing basic education and skills to needy women and also to benefit 
widows, destitute deserted women and also those belonging to economically 
backward classes. Under the Scheme, grant is given to voluntary organisations 
for conducting courses of two-year duration for preparing candidates for primary, 
middle and matric level examinations and one-year duration for matric failed 
candidates. 
4. Vocational Training Programme 
Based on the national policy on skill development for girls and women 
the Central Social Welfare Board had started the Scheme of the Vocational 
Training Programme in the year 1975 to train women in marketable trades and 
also to upgrade their sk ills in order to enable and empower them to access 
remunerative employment opportunities, which will enhance their self-confidence 
and self-esteem. The Training Programme is organised in rural, tribal, backward, 
urban slum areas through Voluntary organisations in the traditional and non-

traditional trades like Computer Training, Community Health Workers, 
Paramedical Vocations, Typing and Shorthand, to enable them to get employment in 
Government, Public Sector Undertakings, Corporations, Autonomous Bodies, Private 
Sector etc. Special emphasis is also laid on implementing this Programme in After 
Care-Homes, Women Cell of Jails and other custodian institutions. The organisations 
are identified through State Social Welfare Advisory Boards in all States/U.Ts. And 
implementation of the training programme is monitored through field machinery. The 
skills of traditional artisans are also being upgraded to provide opportunities for 
self-employment. The Scheme has been instrumental in providing job opportunities 
to a large number of needy women and thereby enhancing their socio-economic 
status. 
5. Awareness Generation Projects for Rural & Poor Women 
The Awareness Generation Programme aims to identify the needs of rural and 
poor women and to generate awareness among them about their status in the family 
and society and to activate mem to work for achieving their rights and to deal with 
social issues. Since 1993-94, special emphasis has been given to participation of 
women in Panchayati Raj institutions and their role in promoting national integration 
and communal harmony. Some of the schemes of the Department of Women & 
Child Development such as the Rashtriya Manila Kosh and the Manila Samridhi 
Yojana have also been included in mis Scheme to motivate rural women towards 
self-reliance. Relevant topics are taken up in a camp of 8 days duration for 25 
beneficiaries, which are followed by 2 days for detailed evaluation of the camp. The 
assessment of the impact of the camp on the beneficiaries and the community is 
done within 6 months on completion of the camp. A sum of Rs. 10,000/- is given to 
an organisation for one Awareness Generation Project. Training of organisers is a 
pre-requisite condition for organising the camps for which a number of training 
centres in every state have been identified by the National Standing Committee and 
CSWB. The expense of Rs. 1000/- per trainee is provided by the Central Social 
Welfare Board. 
6. Socio- economic Programme 
The Socio-Economic Programme of th e Central Social Welfare Board 
endeavors to provide employment opportunities on full or part time basis to 
destitute women, widows, deserted and the physically handicapped, to 
supplement their meager family income. Besides, women entrepreneurs are 
encouraged to exhibit and sell their income. Besides, women entrepreneurs are 
encouraged to exhibit and sell their products through Exhibition-cum-Melas

organised by State Boards at Distt. level. The Central Social Welfare has two different 
types of schemes of assistance under this Programme as follows: 
• Agro - based Units 
The Central Social Welfare Board assists voluntary organisatons for setting up agro-
based units like dairy, poultry, piggery, goatery etc. for poor and needy women. 
However, for the past few years' proposals for Agro-based Units were not 
considered. 
• Production Units 
Voluntary organisations are encouraged to set up Production Units, which can 
provide employment on full or part time basis to women. Project proposals should 
be cleared by District Industrial Centres, KVICs etc. who look into viability of the 
projects. A gram is provided by the Central Social Welfare Board to facilitate 
setting up a Production Unit by the grantee institution. 
7. Education Work for Prevention of Atrocities on Women 
The scheme of assistance to voluntary organizations for Education Work for 
Prevention of Atrocities on Women was started in 1982. Under this scheme, universities, 
colleges, women studies centres, institutions of higher learning and voluntary

Empowerment Project, was sanctioned on 16-10-1998 as a Centrally-sponsored

9. Integrated Women's Empowerment Programme (Swayamsidha) 
Swayamsidha is an Integrated scheme for women's empowerment. It is based 
on formation of women into Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and aims at holistic 
empowerment of women through awareness generation, economic empowerment and 
convergence of various schemes. 
The vision of Swayamsidha is to mobilize and develop empowered women 
who will: 
• Demand their rights from family, community and government; 
• Have increased access to, and control over, material, social and political 
resources; 
• Have enhanced awareness and improved skills ; and 
• Be able to raise issues of common concern through mobilization and 
networking. 
As a result of Swyamsidha, the nature of changes envisaged are expected to result 
in self-reliant and sustainable institutions, which priorities women's needs and interests 
and bring about their social and economic empowerment. These institutions should 
be ready in the last year to take over the role of implementers to ensure complete 
sustainability of the approach even after completion of Swyamsidha.

The scheme has been designed with a flexible and innovative approach to 
cater to the requirement of various types of women in distress in diverse situations 
under different conditions. The scheme provides shelter, counselling and training 
for women in difficult circumstances who do not have any social and economic 
support.

Constitution of India under Article 45 envisaged provision of free and compulsory

compulsory education for all children up to the age of 14. Suitable programmes should

launched a number of programmes/schemes like Operation Blackboard, Teacher

and State Specific Projects such as Lok Jumbish and Shikha Karmi Project in Rajasthan,

Pradesh.

isation of elementary education. During the period 1950-51 to 1999-2000, the number 
of primary schools has increased by more than 3 times from 2.10 lakh in 1950-51 to 
6.42 lakh in 1999-2000 whereas the number of upper primary shcools increased 15 
times from 13,600 in 1950-51 to 1,98,000 in 1999-2000 
The enrolment at primary stage has increased by 5.91 times between 1950-51 and 
1999-2000, and for girls the increase was 9.16 times. At the upper primary level, the 
increase in enrolment during this period was more than 13 times, and in the case of girls 
the increase was about 33 times. The average annual growth

in November, 2000 to pursue universal elementary education in a mission mode.
